title: Public Speaking - The Art of Rhetoric
author: UI-TARS Team
description: How to speak with confidence, persuade others, and tell a great story
learningObjectives: Understand the 3 Pillars of Rhetoric (Ethos, Pathos, Logos)

2-5.title: Show and Tell!
2-5.description: Let's share our favorite things with our friends!

en.title: Show and Tell!
en.welcome: Do you have a favorite toy? A favorite rock? Let's show it to everyone!
en.mainContent:
**What is Show and Tell?**
*   **Show:** Hold up your toy so everyone can see. 'Look at my dinosaur!'
*   **Tell:** Say something about it. 'He is green and he roars!'

**Speaking Up:**
*   Use your **Big Voice**! Not a whisper. Not a yell. Just big and strong.
*   Look at your friends. Smile! :)

**Listening:**
*   When a friend is talking, we listen. 
*   We use 'Listening Ears.' 
*   We don't interrupt. Shhh.

**Feeling Shy:**
*   It's okay to feel shy. Everyone feels shy sometimes.
*   Take a deep breath. In... Out...
*   You are brave!

**Practice:**
*   Stand up tall like a superhero.
*   Say 'Hello, my name is [Your Name]!'
keyPoints: Show and Tell is sharing things we love
Use a Big Voice so people can hear
Look at your friends and smile
Listen when others are talking
It's okay to be shy; take a deep breath
interactionPrompts: What toy would you bring to Show and Tell?
Show me your 'Listening Ears'.
Stand tall like a superhero!
en.wisdomMoment: Your voice is special. We want to hear what you have to say.
en.cta: Practice Show and Tell with your stuffed animals. They are a great audience!
en.summary: You learned about Show and Tell, Big Voice, Listening, Shyness, and Being Brave!

es.title: ¡Mostrar y Contar!

6-12.title: Public Speaking: Be a Star Speaker
6-12.description: How to give a speech without fainting

en.title: Public Speaking: Be a Star Speaker
en.welcome: Did you know that most people are more scared of Public Speaking than they are of spiders? It's true! But it's a superpower you can learn.
en.mainContent:
**The 3 Secrets of Speaking:**
1.  **Eye Contact:** Don't look at the floor. Look at the people! Pick 3 people in the room and look at them one by one.
2.  **Volume:** Speak loud enough for the person in the back row to hear you. Imagine throwing your voice like a ball.
3.  **Body Language:** Stand up straight. Don't wiggle. Keep your hands out of your pockets. You look confident (even if you are nervous!).

**Structuring Your Speech:**
*   **The Hook:** Start with something cool. A joke? A question? A scary fact? Grab their attention!
*   **The Meat:** The middle part. Tell your story. Give your facts.
*   **The Conclusion:** The end. Remind them what you said. Say 'Thank You.'

**Dealing with Nerves:**
*   Butterflies in your tummy? That's just energy! 
*   Take 3 deep breaths before you start.
*   Remember: The audience *wants* you to do well. They are on your side.

**Practice:** Practice in front of a mirror. Practice in front of your dog. The more you do it, the easier it gets.
keyPoints: Eye Contact connects you to the audience
Volume: Throw your voice to the back row
Body Language: Stand tall, no wiggling
Structure: Hook -> Meat -> Conclusion
Nerves are normal; breathe through them
interactionPrompts: Give me a 'Hook' for a speech about Pizza. (e.g., 'Did you know Americans eat 350 slices of pizza every second?')
Show me 'Confident Body Language'. Now show me 'Nervous Body Language'.
Why shouldn't you read your speech from a paper?
en.wisdomMoment: Courage is not the absence of fear. It is acting in spite of it. (Mark Twain). You can be scared and still speak.
en.core_metaphor: Speech is a gift you give the audience
en.cta: Write a 1-minute speech about your favorite hobby. Perform it for your family tonight.
en.summary: You've learned about Eye Contact, Volume, Body Language, Speech Structure, and Nerves.

13-17.title: Rhetoric: The Art of Persuasion
13-17.description: Ethos, Pathos, Logos, and how to win an argument

en.title: Rhetoric: The Art of Persuasion
en.welcome: Aristotle defined Rhetoric as 'the art of discovering all the available means of persuasion.' Whether you are asking for a raise or running for President, you need Rhetoric.
en.mainContent:
**The Rhetorical Triangle:**
1.  **Ethos (Credibility):** Why should I trust you? 
    *   *Example:* 'As a doctor with 20 years of experience...'
    *   *Tip:* Dress the part. Speak with confidence. Cite sources.
2.  **Pathos (Emotion):** How do you make me feel? 
    *   *Example:* Showing a picture of a sad puppy to get donations.
    *   *Tip:* Tell stories. Use vivid language. Connect to their values.
3.  **Logos (Logic):** Does it make sense? 
    *   *Example:* 'Statistics show that 90% of users...'
    *   *Tip:* Use facts, data, and clear reasoning.

**The Best Arguments Use All Three:** If you have Logic but no Emotion, you are boring. If you have Emotion but no Logic, you are manipulative. If you have no Ethos, no one listens.

**Fallacies (Bad Logic):** Watch out for these!
*   **Ad Hominem:** Attacking the person, not the argument. ('You're stupid!').
*   **Straw Man:** Attacking a fake version of the argument. ('You hate animals!' when they just said they don't like cats).
*   **Bandwagon:** 'Everyone is doing it!'

**The Power of the Pause:** Silence is loud. Pausing before a big point makes people lean in. It shows confidence.
keyPoints: Rhetoric is the art of persuasion
Ethos = Credibility (Trust me)
Pathos = Emotion (Feel this)
Logos = Logic (Think this)
Avoid Logical Fallacies (Ad Hominem, Straw Man)
Silence is a powerful rhetorical tool
interactionPrompts: Try to persuade me to eat broccoli using Pathos (Emotion).
Now persuade me using Logos (Logic).
Why is 'Ad Hominem' a bad way to argue?
en.wisdomMoment: Speech is power: speech is to persuade, to convert, to compel. (Ralph Waldo Emerson). Use your power for good.
en.cta: Watch a famous speech (MLK's 'I Have a Dream'). Identify the Ethos, Pathos, and Logos. (Hint: It's mostly Pathos!).
en.summary: You've explored Ethos, Pathos, Logos, Logical Fallacies, and the Power of the Pause.

18-35.title: Advanced Public Speaking: Storytelling & Presence
18-35.description: TED Talk secrets, vulnerability, and owning the room

en.title: Advanced Public Speaking: Storytelling & Presence
en.welcome: Information alone is forgettable. Stories are unforgettable. To be a great speaker, you must stop presenting and start storytelling.
en.mainContent:
**The TED Talk Formula:**
1.  **One Big Idea:** Don't cover 10 topics. Cover one idea deeply. Give it a catchy name.
2.  **The Hero's Journey:** Frame your talk as a journey. 'I used to think X... then Y happened... now I know Z.'
3.  **Vulnerability:** Be human. Admit a failure. Share a fear. Perfection creates distance; vulnerability creates connection (Brené Brown).

**Presence (Charisma):** 
*   **Grounding:** Feel your feet on the floor. Don't pace nervously.
*   **Open Posture:** Expose your heart (literally). No crossed arms. It signals safety and openness.
*   **Voice Modulation:** Vary your pitch and speed. Monotone puts the brain to sleep. Whisper for secrets; boom for passion.

**Handling Q&A:** 
*   The Q&A is where you win the audience. 
*   *Tip:* Repeat the question (gives you time to think). 
*   *Tip:* If you don't know, say 'I don't know, but I'll find out.' Honesty beats BS.

**Visual Aids (Death by PowerPoint):** 
*   Slides are for *images*, not text. 
*   If the audience is reading your slide, they aren't listening to you. 
*   You are the presentation, not the slides.
keyPoints: Focus on One Big Idea
Use Storytelling (Hero's Journey) to structure your talk
Vulnerability creates connection
Presence comes from grounding and open posture
Slides should be visual, not text-heavy (No Death by PowerPoint)
interactionPrompts: What is your 'One Big Idea' that you want to share with the world?
Practice standing in 'Power Pose' (Wonder Woman). How does it feel?
Tell a 30-second story about a time you failed. (Vulnerability practice).
en.wisdomMoment: They may forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel. (Maya Angelou).
en.cta: Record yourself speaking for 2 minutes. Watch it back with the sound OFF. What is your body saying?
en.summary: You've explored TED Formula, Vulnerability, Presence, Voice Modulation, Q&A, and Visual Aids.

36-60.title: Communication Skills: Listening and Conflict
36-60.description: Active listening, non-violent communication, and difficult conversations

en.title: Communication Skills: Listening and Conflict
en.welcome: We spend years learning to read and write, but how much time learning to listen? Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply.
en.mainContent:
**Active Listening:** 
*   **Eye Contact:** Look at them.
*   **Mirroring:** Repeat back what they said. 'So what I'm hearing is...'
*   **Validation:** 'It makes sense that you feel that way.' You don't have to agree to validate.

**Non-Violent Communication (NVC):** A framework for conflict (Marshall Rosenberg).
1.  **Observation:** 'When you leave your socks on the floor...' (Fact, not judgment).
2.  **Feeling:** '...I feel frustrated...'
3.  **Need:** '...because I need order in the house.'
4.  **Request:** 'Would you be willing to put them in the hamper?'

**Difficult Conversations:** 
*   Don't have them over text! Text removes tone and creates misunderstanding.
*   Use 'I' statements ('I feel...') instead of 'You' statements ('You always...'). 'You' statements trigger defensiveness.

**The Pause:** When you are angry, your IQ drops 20 points. Pause. Breathe. Respond, don't react.
keyPoints: Active Listening involves Mirroring and Validation
NVC Formula: Observation -> Feeling -> Need -> Request
Avoid 'You' statements (Accusatory); use 'I' statements (Vulnerable)
Never have difficult conversations over text
Pause when angry to regain your intelligence
interactionPrompts: Practice an 'I Statement' for something that annoys you.
Why is it harder to listen than to talk?
Try to 'Mirror' the next thing someone says to you.
en.wisdomMoment: Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom. (Viktor Frankl).
en.cta: Have a conversation today where you ask 3 follow-up questions before you share your own opinion. Be a detective of the other person.
en.summary: You've explored Active Listening, NVC, I-Statements, Texting Rules, and The Pause.

61-102.title: The Art of Conversation: Connection in a Digital Age
61-102.description: Reclaiming the lost art of face-to-face talk

en.title: The Art of Conversation: Connection in a Digital Age
en.welcome: Conversation is the most human thing we do. It is how we bond, learn, and love. But in a world of screens, we are forgetting how to talk.
en.mainContent:
**The Death of Conversation:** We prioritize efficiency over connection. A text is faster than a call. An emoji is faster than a sentence. But efficiency kills intimacy.

**Small Talk:** It gets a bad rap, but it is the 'on-ramp' to deep talk. You can't start with 'What is the meaning of life?' You start with the weather to establish safety.

**Deep Talk:** Moving beyond the weather. 
*   *Ask Open-Ended Questions:* Not 'Did you have a good day?' (Yes/No). Ask 'What was the best part of your day?'
*   *Be Curious:* Assume everyone you meet knows something you don't.

**The Phone Stack:** When out to dinner, everyone puts their phone in the middle of the table. First one to touch their phone pays the bill. Reclaim the table.

**Listening as a Gift:** Giving someone your full, undivided attention is the greatest gift you can give. It says 'You matter.'

**Storytelling:** Elders are the keepers of the family stories. If you don't tell them, they disappear. Tell your grandkids about your first car, your first love, your biggest mistake.
keyPoints: Efficiency kills intimacy; conversation takes time
Small Talk is the necessary bridge to Deep Talk
Ask Open-Ended Questions to spark dialogue
Put the phone away to show respect
Listening is an act of love
Share your stories before they are lost
interactionPrompts: What is your 'Go-To' question to start a conversation?
Do you feel annoyed when someone checks their phone while you are talking?
What story do you want your family to remember?
en.wisdomMoment: Conversation is a game of catch. You throw the ball (speak), they catch it and throw it back (reply). Don't hold the ball too long.
en.cta: Call a friend today. Don't text. Call. Hear their voice. Notice the difference.
en.summary: You've explored The Death of Conversation, Small Talk, Deep Talk, Phone Stack, Listening, and Storytelling.
